name: Battle of Puebla
info: French troops under Charles de Lorencez failed three times to storm the Mexican forts of Loreto and Guadalupe above Puebla on 5 May 1862, during the second French intervention in Mexico, and withdrew to Orizaba to await reinforcements.

facts.place: The hills of Loreto and Guadalupe overlooking the city of Puebla de los Ángeles (now Puebla), Mexico
facts.sides: France under General Charles de Lorencez, with 6,000 troops; the Mexican Republican Army, with Ignacio Zaragoza giving the orders on the field, in the forts held by the division of Arteaga under General Miguel Negrete.
facts.outcome: The French columns were repulsed and returned to their camp at Los Alamos at seven in the evening, then retired to Orizaba on 8 May to await reinforcements. Lorencez was later dismissed.

t: Lorencez led 6,000 French troops against Puebla, certain that France would win the war in Mexico quickly, and chose to storm the most heavily armed and fortified point.
The French had long rifles against Mexican muskets described as antiquated, but three uphill attacks on the forts of Guadalupe and Loreto failed and the French withdrew after a day of fighting.
The French won the Second Battle of Puebla on 17 May 1863 and went on to take Mexico City, so the victory of 5 May 1862 delayed the invasion without ending it.
dyk: Cinco de Mayo is not the national day of Mexico, as is often believed in the United States. The most important national patriotic holiday there is Independence Day, on 16 September.
ev: President Benito Juárez imposes a two-year moratorium on loan-interest payments to French, British and Spanish creditors
A Spanish fleet takes possession of Veracruz, and French and British forces arrive in January
The agreements among the allies at Orizaba break down, and the French defeat a small Mexican force at Escamela and capture Orizaba
Lorencez's columns fail to storm the forts of Guadalupe and Loreto above Puebla
The French retire to Orizaba to await reinforcements from France
Juárez declares the anniversary of the battle a national holiday
The French win the Second Battle of Puebla and push on to Mexico City

sections.background:
The French intervention in Mexico, at first backed by the United Kingdom and Spain, followed President Benito Juárez's imposition of a two-year moratorium on loan-interest payments from July 1861 to French, British and Spanish creditors. A Spanish fleet took possession of Veracruz on 14 December 1861, and French and British forces arrived on 7 January 1862. On 10 January the Spanish general Juan Prim issued a manifesto disavowing rumours that the allies had come to conquer or to impose a new government; the three powers, it said, wanted only to negotiate their claims. An agreement ratified on 23 January moved the forces inland for a conference at Orizaba and recognised the government of Juárez and Mexican sovereignty.

On 9 April 1862 the agreements at Orizaba broke down, as France made it increasingly clear that it meant to invade Mexico and interfere in its government, in violation of earlier treaties. The British said they would leave and settled their claims by arrangement with the Mexican government. On 11 April the Mexican foreign minister, Manuel Doblado, told the French that their intentions would lead to war. On 16 April the French issued a proclamation inviting Mexicans to join them in setting up a new government, and Juan Almonte, brought back to Mexico by the French, issued a manifesto assuring Mexicans of French good intentions. The French defeated a small Mexican force at Escamela and captured Orizaba. Generals Porfirio Díaz and Ignacio Zaragoza fell back to El Ingenio and then towards Puebla, and on 28 April the French moved on Puebla.
sections.forces:
General Charles de Lorencez led 6,000 French troops against Puebla de los Ángeles, certain that the French would win the war in Mexico quickly. For the attack he formed a column of two battalions of zouaves, a battery under Captain Bernard and four pieces of Captain Mallat's marine artillery. The regiment of marine infantry and the marine riflemen were the reserve, with a mountain gun, and were to guard the rear of the columns against Mexican cavalry on the right. L'Heriller's four battalions of marine infantry guarded the convoy against a Mexican force threatening the left. The French had long rifles that could easily outgun the antiquated muskets of the Mexicans.

The French and Mexican troops under Antonio Taboada, a Mexican officer who collaborated with them, reached Amozoc on 2 May and camped within sight of Puebla on the 4th. Lorencez meant to take the forts of Loreto and Guadalupe at once, as their possession would give him the city. Almonte and Antonio de Haro y Tamariz had advised an attack on an orchard of the Convento del Carmen opposite the fortified heights, or simply bypassing Puebla and marching on the capital; neither was done. Francisco Bulnes, a Mexican historian, remarked that Lorencez lacked the men to starve the city out and the artillery to take it by intimidation or gradual assaults.

The Mexican Republican Army reached Puebla on 3 May. On the 4th Arteaga's division, now under General Miguel Negrete, occupied the forts of Guadalupe and Loreto and the rest of the force took quarters in the city. The Mexican strength is not known.
sections.course:
At half past eleven Lorencez arranged his attack column. The two battalions of zouaves left their backpacks at the foot of the hill and climbed in columns, with ten pieces of horse artillery, bearing right towards Fort Guadalupe. According to a report telegraphed by Zaragoza to the central government, the fighting broke out at noon. Zaragoza saw that the French meant to attack the most fortified and heavily armed point directly, and ordered both forts reinforced. The French halted opposite Guadalupe and shelled both forts for two hours, then a strong column preceded by sharpshooters advanced on Guadalupe from the north. Felipe Berriozábal was ordered to reinforce the two hills.

In the first attack the French met little opposition until halfway up, where two Mexican battalions exchanged fire with the sharpshooters and fell back. When the column turned diagonally to the right, as if to go between the forts, both forts fired on it. Attacked from all sides, the French retreated and were pursued until another French column came to their support.

The two columns then pushed on together towards Guadalupe, combined and split into three. This second attack, on the east and north of the city, was much more vigorous. The two columns that tried the hill from the north were routed, and General Díaz with part of his brigade and two pieces of artillery drove back the columns marching on the Mexican positions. The third column, reaching the east side as the others were repulsed, was also defeated, and Mexican cavalry charged the rest and prevented them from reorganising. The two sides faced each other until seven in the evening, when the French returned to their camp at Los Alamos.
sections.aftermath:
The French went back to Orizaba on 8 May to await reinforcements on their way from France. The French are said to have retired after significant casualties. Zaragoza received the thanks of the Mexican congress and was awarded a sword, the city of Puebla de los Ángeles was renamed Puebla de Zaragoza, and honours were decreed for those who took part. Zaragoza sent the government the medals and decorations taken on the field and from prisoners, but Juárez returned them together with the French prisoners of war. Zaragoza died four months later of typhoid.

The French attributed their defeat to a wider lack of support from the Conservative Party. Two days after the battle General Taboada, who had collaborated with the French, wrote to his liberal friend Tomás O'Horán inviting him to join them, arguing that they wished to establish a stable government and bring order. O'Horán refused and fought against the French at the siege of Puebla the following year, but later defected to the forces of the Second Mexican Empire.

Napoleon III sent more troops to Mexico and dismissed Lorencez. Under General Élie Frédéric Forey the French won the Second Battle of Puebla on 17 May 1863 and pushed on to Mexico City. When the capital fell, Juárez's government went into exile in the remote north of the country. With French backing the Habsburg Archduke Maximilian became Emperor of Mexico. Porfirio Díaz, who had played a notable part in the battle, was captured and escaped, remained a leading liberal commander of the intervention, and became President of Mexico in 1876.
sections.sources: The account of the day rests in part on a report telegraphed by Zaragoza to the central government, which puts the start of the fighting at noon. The Mexican historian Francisco Bulnes judged that Lorencez could hardly have hoped to storm the city with the men and artillery he had, and the advice that Almonte and Haro y Tamariz gave Lorencez, which he did not take, is part of the record of the days before the battle. Taboada's letter to O'Horán two days after the battle shows how the French case was put to Mexican liberals.
sections.legacy:
The battle was an inspiration to Mexico during the war and a revelation to a world that had largely expected a quick victory for French arms. It filled Juárez's government with high hopes. On 9 May 1862 Juárez declared the anniversary a national holiday, the Battle of Puebla Day or Battle of Cinco de Mayo. It is celebrated chiefly in the state of Puebla, with some limited recognition elsewhere in Mexico. Cinco de Mayo is not the national day of Mexico: the most important patriotic holiday is Independence Day on 16 September, which commemorates the call to arms of 1810 that began the War of Independence. Since the 1930s a re-enactment of the battle has been held each year at Peñón de los Baños, a rocky outcrop near Mexico City International Airport.

In the United States the day grew into a celebration of Mexican heritage. The Good Neighbor Policy of President Franklin D. Roosevelt, meant to promote links with Latin American nations and peoples, was one of the key factors in its spread, and it gained popularity in the 1950s and 1960s. The first celebrations were local, among Mexican immigrants from the state of Puebla commemorating the battle. Over time the origins became less emphasised, and the date became a general celebration of Mexican culture by immigrants and their descendants from all parts of Mexico. A comparable change is seen in St Patrick's Day, which has moved from a church holiday marking the arrival of Christianity in Ireland to a largely secular celebration of Irish American culture.

summary: On 5 May 1862 French troops under Lorencez failed three times to storm the Mexican forts above Puebla and withdrew to Orizaba. The French won the Second Battle of Puebla in 1863, but the earlier victory is the origin of the holiday of Cinco de Mayo.
notes: The article gives no Mexican strength and no casualty figures for either side; the forces and aftermath sections say so rather than guess.

Left out as garbled or unsupported: 'A well-armed French warship invaded Veracruz late in 1861 ... forcing President Juarez and his administration into exile' (contradicts the rest of the article); Zaragoza 'a Texas native' and a Mexican force that 'included 500 other Tejanos' (the Celebration section, unsupported by the rest of the article); 'miserably failed' and 'loud bugle cries and complex bayonet drills' to intimidate civilians; the claim that many French did not assemble their weapons.
The article says the pro-French Taboada's troops reached Amozoc with the French on 2 May; the wording is the article's and the role of Taboada's force is unclear.

Who commanded on the Mexican side is not stated outright; Zaragoza is the general who reports and gives orders, and Negrete commanded the forts' division. Brigade names (Díaz, Berriozábal, Álvarez, Trujano, Félix Díaz) appear without ranks beyond those given.

The article says the French attack began on Guadalupe from the east in one paragraph and the north in another; the course follows its order. The French 'retreat' after the first attack and the 'two columns combined and split into three' are the article's wording.

Forey is named only in the lead as taking the city, where the article does not mention the 1863 siege command otherwise; the aftermath attributes the Second Battle of Puebla to the French under Forey on that basis.
The sources section is short because the article names few accounts.
